title: Default Address Selection for Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6)
summary: Describes algorithms for choosing a source address and a destination address in IPv6. They give default behavior for all IPv6 implementations, without overriding choices made by applications or upper-layer protocols. This matters when a host has several addresses and a destination has several to try. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6724 defines default rules for choosing Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) addresses for sending and receiving. Administrators can change the policy, and an application's explicit legal choice takes priority.

subtitle: The default rules IPv6 nodes use to choose source and destination addresses.

tldr.problem: A node can have several source addresses, and a name lookup can return several IPv4 and IPv6 destinations. Common defaults make the resulting choices more predictable.
tldr.mechanism: One ordered algorithm selects a source address and another sorts destination addresses. Both use address properties and a configurable policy table.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6724 obsoletes RFC 3484 and sets default address-selection behavior for IPv6 nodes, including hosts and routers.

today: RFC 6724 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3484. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 6724.

sections.title: Why Address Selection Needs Rules
sections.content:
An IPv6 interface can have several addresses with different scopes, states, or purposes. A name lookup may also return both IPv4 and IPv6 destinations, so a node needs a predictable way to choose which address to use first.

RFC 6724 defines separate source and destination algorithms. The algorithms provide defaults for IPv6 nodes and do not override an application's explicit choice of a legal source or destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer may have several addresses available for one connection. These rules give it a consistent way to choose a sending address and order possible destinations.

sections.title: Where the Two Algorithms Apply
sections.content:
An application may receive a list of destination addresses from an API such as getaddrinfo(). The destination algorithm sorts that list, including IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. The network layer uses the source algorithm when the application has not selected a source address.

The rules compare address pairs in order. They favor suitable scope and configuration, avoid deprecated source addresses, and use the longest common prefix when earlier rules do not decide.
sections.plainLanguage: The application gets a sorted list of places to connect to. The network layer separately chooses which of its own addresses to use when the application leaves that choice open.

sections.title: The Policy Table
sections.content:
The policy table is a longest-prefix lookup table. For each address, it supplies a precedence used to order destinations and a label used to match source and destination prefixes. Implementations SHOULD let administrators configure a table at least as powerful as the one in the RFC.

The default table gives native IPv6 a higher precedence than IPv4 when matching source addresses are available. Administrators can change the table to prefer IPv4 or to handle local network policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy table assigns a priority and label to address prefixes. Administrators can change these values to fit their network, including choosing whether IPv4 or IPv6 should come first.

sections.title: Choosing a Source Address
sections.content:
The source algorithm first forms a set of addresses that could be used for a destination. A source explicitly selected by an application must be respected if it is in that set; otherwise, the network layer treats the choice as an error.

The algorithm applies eight comparison rules as ordered tie-breakers. It prefers the same address as the destination, an appropriate scope, non-deprecated addresses, home addresses, the outgoing interface, a matching label, temporary addresses, and finally a longest matching prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The system compares possible sending addresses using a fixed sequence of rules. It stops when a rule identifies the preferred address; the application can request a different privacy preference for its own choice.

sections.title: Ordering Destination Addresses
sections.content:
The destination algorithm sorts IPv4 and IPv6 addresses together. It applies ten rules in order, starting by avoiding unreachable destinations or ones without a usable source address. Later rules compare scope, deprecated state, home-address status, labels, policy precedence, native transport, and common prefixes.

The final rule preserves the original order if no earlier rule decides. Implementations may use other information to supersede the final prefix and original-order rules. Cached destination ordering must be no more than one second out of date.
sections.plainLanguage: The system sorts possible destinations by applying ten rules, starting with whether a destination can be reached. If the earlier rules do not choose a winner, it uses prefix similarity and then keeps the original order.

sections.title: Security, Privacy, and Status
sections.content:
Source selection can reveal relationships among a node's addresses when another node sends requests that cause replies to choose a source. The default preference for temporary addresses helps reduce this concern. Policy settings can also affect which network path traffic uses, so administrators should protect them from unauthorized changes.

RFC 6724 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3484. The batch metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.
sections.plainLanguage: The address a computer chooses can reveal information and affect the route traffic takes. The RFC recommends protecting policy settings and notes that temporary addresses can reduce some privacy exposure.

viz.caption: DESTINATION ADDRESS RULES, APPLIED IN ORDER

items.label: Avoid unusable destinations
items.desc: Prefer a destination known to be reachable and with a source available.

items.label: Match scope
items.desc: Prefer a destination whose scope matches its selected source.

items.label: Prefer home addresses
items.desc: Use the selected source's home-address status.

items.label: Match labels
items.desc: Prefer matching source and destination labels.

items.label: Native transport
items.desc: Prefer a destination not reached through encapsulation.

items.label: Longest matching prefix
items.desc: Compare within the same address family.

items.label: Keep original order
items.desc: Use the order supplied to the algorithm.
